title: Bhavananda Raya
html:
“You Are Pandu”

Sri Bhavananda Raya was an Oriya devotee, the father of Ramananda Raya and of four more sons whom Mahaprabhu called His eternal servants. In the “Charitamrita” his name appears in several forms: “Raya Bhavananda” (Adi 10.131; Madhya 10.50), “Bhavananda Raya” (Antya 9.15, 9.61, 9.103) and simply “Bhavananda” (Antya 9.120); Kavi Karnapura too calls him so, both in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and in his poem on the Lord. Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami, enumerating the branches of the tree of Sri Chaitanya, places him beside two brahmanas of Nilachala:

“Then come Kashi Mishra, Pradyumna Mishra and Bhavananda Raya, whose company gave the Lord great joy.” (CC, Adi 10.131)

In the numbering of the branches adopted in our edition of the “Charitamrita,” Bhavananda Raya is the seventh branch, and his five sons headed by Ramananda are the eighth. And at once Kaviraja recalls the words the Lord spoke to Bhavananda at their first meeting:

“Embracing him, the Lord said, ‘You are Pandu, and your sons are the five Pandavas: Ramananda Raya, Gopinatha Pattanayaka, Kalanidhi, Sudhanidhi and Vaninatha Nayaka. These five sons of yours are dear to Me, and between Ramananda and Me there is a difference of body alone.’” (CC, Adi 10.132–134)1

The Lord said it plainly: “You are Pandu.” This is no tale of rebirth in the worldly sense: the Lord Himself revealed the eternal nature of His associate. He who in the pastimes of Krishna was Pandu, the father of the five Pandavas, in the pastimes of Gaura appeared as Raya Bhavananda and came with his sons to serve the Lord. Kaviraja describes this meeting in detail in the Madhya-lila, and there the Lord names his wife too as Kunti. On this word of the Lord rests the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” as well. It has no verse of its own on Bhavananda: he is mentioned only where Karnapura discusses the nature of Ramananda and disagrees with those who see Lalita in him:

“Some call him Lalita, but this is accepted by only a few: for Gaura said to Bhavananda: ‘You are Prithapati.’” (GGD 122)

Prithapati is “the husband of Pritha,” that is, of Kunti: it is Pandu. If the father is Pandu, the son is Arjuna, the Pandava; thus the Lord's word to the father became for Karnapura the key to the nature of the son (more on this in the article on Ramananda Raya).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati understands these words in the same way. In his “Anubhashya” on the verse about the branches of the tree he says briefly of Bhavananda: the father of Ramananda Raya, he lived by Brahmagiri, or Alalanatha, was by birth of the shaukra-karanas, and in the pastimes of Krishna is known as King Pandu.

Family and Village

Bhavananda belonged to the karanas, an Oriya community of officials similar to the kayasthas of Bengal; in the “Anubhashya” his family is named more precisely as “shaukra-karana.” Oriya society counts the karanas among the shudras, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta says so plainly. But a Vaishnava stands above every varna: not for nothing did the Lord make Bhavananda's son Ramananda, born in this community, a teacher of sannyasis and panditas.

Bhavananda lived in Orissa, by the ancient holy place of Alalanatha, or Brahmagiri, six kroshas west of Puri2. More precisely, his house stood in the village of Bentpur, about a mile from Alalanatha, and he was a landholder there. His descendants live in Bentpur to this day and bear the family title “Chaudhuri Pattanayaka.” When Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati visited Alalanatha in the year 1337 of the Bengali era (about 1930), the local people told him that Ramananda Raya had been born in this house in Bentpur and that the Lord used to come to Brahmagiri every year; more on this tradition will be found in the article on Ramananda Raya.

Near Bhavananda's house in Bentpur, according to one of the biographies, Madhavi-devi, the sister of Shikhi Mahiti, began the service of the Deity Sri Gopinatha, and He is served there to this day. The same biography calls Shikhi Mahiti the son of Bhavananda Raya's brother, which would make Madhavi-devi his niece too3.

The sources have not preserved the name of Bhavananda's wife. We know only what the Lord called her: “Your wife is Kunti” (CC, Madhya 10.53). They had five sons: Ramananda Raya, Gopinatha Pattanayaka, Kalanidhi, Sudhanidhi and Vaninatha Pattanayaka. Ramananda was the firstborn (CC, Madhya 10.50); Gopinatha, by the order of the names in the “Charitamrita,” the biographies consider the second. And all five were dear to Mahaprabhu — He said so to their father Himself.

What Bhavananda himself was like, his son told best. In the prologue to his drama “Jagannatha-vallabha,” Ramananda Raya, through the stage-director, calls himself “son of Sri Bhavananda Raya, an ocean of jewel-virtues such as serenity”; the father's counsels, “steeped in the many maxims of policy laid down by the preceptor of the gods,” Brihaspati, made the king upright and virtuous. The Sanskrit here is partly corrupt, and the compound can also be read otherwise: then it is Bhavananda himself who is called “lord of the earth,” a ruler. Relying on this prologue, the biographies say that Bhavananda was versed in all branches of learning and endowed with every virtue.

The Utkal poet Govinda-deva in his poem “Sri Gaura-krishnodaya” (1758) portrays him thus: “the learned Bhavananda Raya, lord of Vidyapura… he who had gladly laid the burden of the kingdom on his firstborn Ramananda and himself lives at home, knowing not the slightest hardship” (11.6)4. Later hymns of praise remember him too: the “Vaishnava-vandana” of Devakinandana says, “I praise Sri Pradyumna Mishra and Raya Bhavananda, I praise Kalanidhi, Sudhanidhi and Gopinatha” (v. 66) — though scholars hold that this couplet was added later, from the “Charitamrita.” And a commentary on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Adi 2.30) names Bhavananda Raya and his sons headed by Ramananda among the devotees born in Utkala; in the “Bhagavata” itself his name does not occur.

The First Meeting

When Mahaprabhu returned to Puri from His long journey through the south, His devotees hastened to see His feet. In the brief summary of those days Kaviraja says that the Lord then met both Shikhi Mahiti and Bhavananda Raya (CC, Madhya 1.130), and he tells of this meeting in detail in the tenth chapter of the Madhya-lila:

“Just then Bhavananda Raya arrived and, with his four sons, fell at Mahaprabhu's feet.” (CC, Madhya 10.49)

The fifth son, Ramananda, was still on the Godavari. Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, introducing the devotees of Nilachala to the Lord, said: “This is Bhavananda Raya. His eldest son is Ramananda Raya.” (CC, Madhya 10.50). Mahaprabhu embraced Bhavananda and began to glorify his son:

“‘The glory of one whose son is a jewel like Ramananda cannot be described in this world. You are Pandu himself, and your wife is Kunti; your five wise sons are the five Pandavas.’” (CC, Madhya 10.52–53)

Kavi Karnapura shows the same scene in the eighth act of his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya.” Sarvabhauma names to the Lord, one after another, the servants of Jagannatha and the devotees of Puri, and, coming to Ramananda's family, says: “These are the brothers of Ramananda Raya, and among them — here is Vaninatha Pattanayaka. And this is their father, Bhavananda Raya.” They all fall prostrate, and Sarvabhauma asks the Lord to accept them as His own.

Bhavananda's reply is a model of Vaishnava humility:

“Raya said, ‘I am a fallen, worldly shudra, yet You touch me — this is the mark of the Lord.’” (CC, Madhya 10.54)

These are the words not of a worldly man but of a devotee whom the Lord had just called Pandu. He was a shudra only by social reckoning, and he called himself “worldly” out of humility — the dainya that adorns every Vaishnava. And in the Lord's touching a “shudra” he sees no breach of propriety, but a sign of His divinity: only the Lord Himself could act so.

And Bhavananda at once gave the Lord all that he had:

“‘Together with my house, my wealth, my servants and my five sons, I have surrendered myself at Your feet. Vaninatha here will stay at Your feet and carry out whatever You order, whenever You order it. Regard me as Your own and do not hold back with me: whatever You wish, whenever You wish it, simply give the order.’” (CC, Madhya 10.55–57)5

And the Lord replied:

“Why should I hold back? You are no stranger. Birth after birth you and your family have been My servants.” (CC, Madhya 10.58)

Having said this, Mahaprabhu embraced Bhavananda again, placed His feet on the heads of his sons and promised that in a few days Ramananda too would come. Vaninatha He kept with Him as His personal servant, and Bhavananda with the other sons He sent home (CC, Madhya 10.59–61). So in one short meeting the whole life of Bhavananda was revealed: he surrendered to the Lord with all his house and family, and heard in reply that he and his family are the Lord's servants birth after birth.

The poets too remember that day in their own way. Kavi Karnapura in the “Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” writes that the Lord was seen by “a noble man of pure mind, virtuous and righteous, named Bhavananda, adorned with streams of joy”; the Lord embraced him firmly with both arms and spoke sweet words to him: “O, you are fortunate like Pandu!”6 His five sons — Ramananda and the others — stayed near the Lord and, serving Him, became very dear to Him, and the gentle, large-hearted Vaninatha, “the unfailing friend of all people,” served Him (13.133–136).

Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” gives the Lord's words thus: “You are Pandu himself with five sons; and you take shelter of Sri Krishna, who is beyond the world — therefore you rightly bear your name” (11.7). Bhavananda answers: “This servant is sold for a drop of Your boundless mercy,” asks leave to return to his land, promising that his eldest son will come in his place, and leaves with the Lord Vaninatha, “the best of counsellors.” After a few days in Puri he sees Jagannatha, honours His prasada and departs for his city (11.8–10).

The Sons with the Lord

The word given that day Bhavananda kept. Vaninatha remained with Mahaprabhu and served Him in Nilachala, and once King Prataparudra himself said of him: “Vaninatha, the son of Bhavananda, is carrying prasada, and five or seven men are going with him” (CC, Madhya 11.108). Ramananda became the Lord's intimate associate (he has an article of his own). Of the other brothers the sources say less, but the Lord regarded all five as His own.

Among those who settled with the Lord in Puri, some editions of the “Charitamrita” also name a certain “Bhavananda” (Madhya 1.253); whether this is Bhavananda Raya the biographies do not say, and he himself, as we have seen, lived in his own village7. His family remained connected with Puri even after the Lord: Ramadasa Vishvasa, having settled there, taught the “Kavya-prakasha” to the Pattanayaka family (CC, Antya 13.111) — our translation explains: “the descendants of Bhavananda Raya.”

Gopinatha on the Changa

The words “with your whole family you are My servant” Bhavananda was to see proved in deed, when trouble came to his second son. Gopinatha Pattanayaka served the king as collector of revenue in the district of Malajathya-Dandapata (now Medinipur, according to the biographies) and fell into arrears to the treasury of two lakhs of kahanas — counted in cowrie shells, more than two hundred and fifty million. The king's eldest son, Prince Purushottama Jana, who was called Bara-Jana, angered by Gopinatha, ordered him raised onto the changa — a scaffold for execution under which naked swords were set, so that the condemned could be thrown down onto them (CC, Antya 9.13–30, 9.99). People, hoping for the Lord's mercy, ran to Him:

“‘They have set swords beneath it and will throw him down onto them from above. Only if You, Lord, protect him will he be saved. Bhavananda Raya and his whole family are Your servants. His son is Your servant, and it is fitting that You protect him.’” (CC, Antya 9.14–15)

But Mahaprabhu, setting the example of a sannyasi's dharma, remained outwardly unconcerned. One who collects revenue in the king's name, He said, must first give the king his due; the king has the right to take what is his — and what can a monk who has renounced the world do? (CC, Antya 9.31–35). Then fresh news came: Vaninatha and others had been taken into custody with the whole family8. Svarupa Damodara and the other devotees fell at the Lord's feet: “‘The family of Ramananda Raya are all Your servants. Such indifference is not fitting for You.’” (CC, Antya 9.37). The Lord answered again that He was a beggar and could do nothing, and showed them the only way:

“‘So if you all have it in mind to save him, go together to the feet of Jagannatha. Jagannatha is Ishvara, the Lord Himself, and all things are in His hands. He is able to do, not to do, or to do otherwise.’” (CC, Antya 9.43–44)

This “unconcern” is not indifference to the devotees, but a pastime and a lesson. A sannyasi who has renounced the world does not meddle in worldly affairs and does not petition kings; and to householders in a ruler's service the Lord gives an instruction: not to spend what belongs to the king on themselves. His mercy, however, works quietly and without His visible part. At that very time Harichandana Patra went to the king and told him everything, and the king replied:

“I know nothing of this. Why should I take his life? It is his money I want. Go there and settle everything, so that the money comes in and his life is spared.” (CC, Antya 9.49–50)

Harichandana conveyed the king's will to Bara-Jana, and Gopinatha was at once taken down from the changa (CC, Antya 9.51). The biographies add that Harichandana was moved to this by the Lord Himself, who dwells in everyone's heart as the Supersoul.

“I Shall Go to Alalanatha”

Soon Kashi Mishra came to the Lord, and Mahaprabhu, as if troubled, said to him:

“‘I cannot stay here; I shall go to Alalanatha. There are many disturbances here, and I find no peace.’” (CC, Antya 9.60)

The family of Bhavananda Raya, the Lord said, manages the king's affairs and spends the king's wealth in various ways, and when the king demands his due, they come to Him; four times people had run to Him with the news that Gopinatha had been raised onto the changa (CC, Antya 9.61–63):

“I am a mendicant sannyasi who lives in solitude, yet they come and pain Me by telling Me their own troubles.” (CC, Antya 9.64)

And at once the Lord asked: today Jagannatha has saved Gopinatha, but who will save him tomorrow, if he does not return the king's money (CC, Antya 9.65)? The Lord speaks these words in the role of a sannyasi, for whom it is not fitting to hear of worldly matters; they teach detachment, but they do not denounce Bhavananda's family. Kashi Mishra long urged Him to stay: “Stay on here. Why should You go to Alalanatha? No one will make You listen to the talk of worldly men.” (CC, Antya 9.78). And at noon, when King Prataparudra came as usual to Kashi Mishra's house, Mishra told him that the Lord meant to leave Puri and go to Alalanatha (CC, Antya 9.80–85).

The king grew sad and at once resolved to forgive Gopinatha the whole debt. Kashi Mishra answered: it is not the remission of the debt that the Lord desires — it is their suffering that He cannot bear (CC, Antya 9.97). And when the king resolved to remit the debt all the same, Mishra warned him that the Lord would be displeased (CC, Antya 9.101). But the king replied:

“I shall give up the money, but do not tell Him that. Let Him know only this: they are naturally dear to me. Bhavananda Raya is worthy of my honour and esteem (pujya-garvita), and I naturally feel affection for his sons.” (CC, Antya 9.102–103)

He remitted the debt, doubled Gopinatha's salary, restored him to his former post and put a silk cloth on him (CC, Antya 9.104–107). And to Kashi Mishra, so that the Lord should not think the debt had been forgiven only for His sake, the king sent word:

“All of Bhavananda's sons are most dear to me; I regard them all as my own self. So I give them posts here and there. They eat, drink, plunder and give away, and I do not look into it.” (CC, Antya 9.120–121)

This is the speech not of a judge about grasping officials, but of a sovereign about his own kin. The king went on: Ramananda he himself had made governor of Rajamahendri; he had not known that his son meant to destroy Gopinatha, for he regards all the sons of Bhavananda Raya as his own family — they are dear to him as it is (CC, Antya 9.122–126). So the king's love for Bhavananda's family became known to all.

Kaviraja stresses that the Lord did not wish Gopinatha's debt to be forgiven, his salary doubled and his post restored; He had only been asked to save Gopinatha from death — and that alone bore such fruit. The Lord's intentions are inconceivable even to Brahma and Shiva (CC, Antya 9.112–115).

“He did not entreat Kashi Mishra, nor did He entreat the king; yet without any effort He gave all this fruit.” (CC, Antya 9.150)

The Lord punished no one: the execution was the scheme of an angry prince and had been cancelled even before Kashi Mishra came, and the whole affair ended not in punishment but in forgiveness of the debt and honours.

Why, then, did the Lord not intervene Himself? Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains: worldly well-being is only a secondary mercy of the Lord; and had Gaurasundara, who appeared in the guise of a renounced devotee, set about helping worldly people with their affairs, imitation of Him would have degraded the ideal of renounced Vaishnavas — therefore a detached, impartial renunciant never takes up worldly business. And the king's remitting the debt for the Lord's sake would have meant, he says, that the Lord had in effect accepted the king's money (“Anubhashya,” Antya 9.117, 9.148).

Bhavananda's Gratitude

When Kashi Mishra had conveyed the king's words to the Lord, Bhavananda Raya came to Mahaprabhu. Together with his five sons he bowed at His feet, and the Lord raised him up and embraced him; thus, says Kaviraja, Ramananda Raya and all his family met the Lord (CC, Antya 9.127–129). And Bhavananda said:

“‘My whole family are Your servants. Saving us in this danger, Lord, You have bought us again for a price (nila mula).’” (CC, Antya 9.130)

Now You have shown Your love for Your devotees, he said, as long ago You saved the five Pandavas from danger (CC, Antya 9.131). The father of the Pandavas recognized in Gaura's mercy the same care with which Krishna had once surrounded his sons.

Then Gopinatha bowed at the Lord's feet — with the silk cloth on his head, the king's gift9:

“He remitted the money I owed and doubled my salary; he gave me my post again and dressed me in silk. <…> On the changa I meditated on Your feet, and by the power of remembering Your feet I obtained this fruit.” (CC, Antya 9.133, 135)

But Gopinatha understood that worldly gains are only a shadow of the true good that remembrance of the Lord's feet bestows, and he prayed for more:

“‘You made Ramananda Raya and Vaninatha free from worldly affairs. But I have not received the mercy that brings this about! Show me pure mercy, Gosani: take away my worldly affairs. I have grown weary of them (nirvinna); worldly affairs are not for me.’” (CC, Antya 9.138–139)

This is the meaning of the whole story. As Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains, the chief fruit of remembering the Lord's feet is love for Him, while life, honour and wealth preserved are only a shadow of that fruit, for everything worldly is by its very nature unstable (“Amrita-pravaha-bhashya,” Antya 9.137).

The Lord answered Gopinatha in words that embraced the whole of Bhavananda's family:

“Whether you manage great worldly affairs or live detached and indifferent to the world, birth after birth you five are My own servants. But keep one order of Mine: do not spend any of the king's principal (mula-dhana). After paying the king his principal, spend whatever profit remains on various pious works.” (CC, Antya 9.141–143)

And He forbade them to spend money on wrongdoing, for that ruins both this life and the next (CC, Antya 9.144). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains these words: one who remembers that he is the Lord's eternal servant is harmed neither by outward renunciation nor by the greatest worldly affairs; one who serves Krishna is a great sannyasi even at home. Trouble comes only when a person forgets this and begins to enjoy for himself (“Anubhashya,” Antya 9.141–144).

People were amazed at the Lord's mercy and could not understand His conduct: for when He had been asked for help, He had said that He could do nothing (CC, Antya 9.147–148). Kaviraja himself calls this story the Lord's “kripa-vivarta” in the house of the Raya, and says that in it His love for His devotees was revealed (CC, Antya 9.145). Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains the word: mercy in the guise of worldly good is not yet true mercy; only to the worldly mind does one thing appear as another, and this is called “vivarta.”

Days of Remembrance

Neither the day, nor the year, nor the place of Bhavananda Raya's appearance and departure is named by the biographies or by the primary sources; nor are his days found in our calendar.

Significance

Bhavananda Raya has remained in the memory of Vaishnavas above all through the Lord's word: “You are Pandu.” The father of the five Pandavas in Krishna's pastimes, he came into Gaura's pastimes together with his sons, and Mahaprabhu, recognizing him at first sight, made him a branch of the tree of Chaitanya and his sons His eternal servants.

His life is one of self-surrender. A noble landholder, father of a governor and of royal officials, he called himself a fallen shudra and gave to the Lord's feet himself, his house, his wealth, his servants and his sons — and one of them for good. In reply he heard that he was no stranger to the Lord and, with his whole family, served Him birth after birth.

And when trouble came to his son, that word was fulfilled. The Lord, keeping the dharma of a sannyasi, did not petition the king or intervene in worldly affairs — yet His mercy, working through the prayer to Jagannatha, through Harichandana and through the king's love, turned the threat of execution into forgiveness and honour. Bhavananda recognized in this the same care with which the Lord had once saved the Pandavas: He does not abandon those who have surrendered to Him. And his son Gopinatha showed why one should remember the Lord: not for worldly gains, but for love of His feet.

Notes

  1. One of the biographies, quoting the verse Adi 10.133, prints “Nayaka Gopinatha” instead of “Nayaka Vaninatha”; the verse number it gives is correct.
  2. A krosha is about two miles, so six kroshas are about twelve miles. Brahmagiri lies to this day some twenty kilometres west of Puri.
  3. Only one biography speaks of this kinship. The “Charitamrita” says only that Madhavi-devi was the sister of Shikhi Mahiti (Adi 10.137), and is silent about any link between their family and Bhavananda.
  4. Only this late poem calls Bhavananda “lord of Vidyapura” who handed the rule to his son. According to the “Charitamrita,” it was King Prataparudra himself who made Ramananda governor of Rajamahendri (Antya 9.122).
  5. One of the biographies renders this request as “regarding me as Your servant”; the Bengali verse has ātmīya-jñāne, “regarding me as Your own, Your kin.”
  6. In Karnapura's poem this is a comparison: “fortunate like Pandu.” We follow the “Charitamrita,” where the Lord says directly: “You are Pandu” (Adi 10.132; Madhya 10.53); on these words rests the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” of the same Karnapura (GGD 122), while the “Gaura-krishnodaya” says: “You are Pandu himself.”
  7. So the verse reads in the Gaudiya Matha edition, in two of the biographies and in the revised translation; the earlier Russian translation had “Bhagavan” at this place. Who this Bhavananda is the sources do not say, and he should not be identified with Bhavananda Raya without reservation.
  8. According to two of the biographies, it was Bhavananda Raya himself with his whole family who was bound and led away; according to the “Charitamrita” (Antya 9.34), Vaninatha and others were taken with the whole family.
  9. The silk cloth is the neta-dhati (CC, Antya 9.107, 9.132–134), a mark of royal honour; in one of the biographies the word is misprinted.
